families.directionality: Two-sided; neither rebound nor decline is the expected direction.
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted next-match win indicator between a transition that follows a loss and one that follows a win.
families.expected_information_reach: Low: a binary outcome with a true effect of a few points needs hundreds of transitions per arm.
families.expected_structural_reach: High — in-session transitions are the most abundant opportunity in the corpus.
families.known_failure_mode: Binary outcome carries almost no information per opportunity, so between-player spread is swamped by sampling noise.
families.name: post_loss_next_outcome
families.opportunity_definition: Every consecutive pair of product-context matches whose gap is at most the session gap.
families.patch_sensitivity: Low; the estimand is a within-player contrast.
families.player_question: After you lose a game, does your next game in the same session go differently from what your context predicts?
families.role_position_breadth: All roles; nothing conditions on position.
families.story_example: "After a loss you win 4 points less often than your own baseline — one of the steeper drops we measure."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows only; both matches inside one 3 h-gap session.
families.why_care: It is the single most discussed idea in Dota self-talk — whether a loss costs you the next game.
families.why_players_differ: Emotional regulation and stop/continue discipline plausibly differ between people in a way a win-rate mean does not capture.

confounders: post-game screen length differing by result
families.directionality: Two-sided; faster and slower are both meaningful.
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted log gap to the next match after a loss versus after a win.
families.expected_information_reach: High: a continuous response with many observations per player.
families.known_failure_mode: Queue-time and party effects are shared across players, so a population-common effect could dominate; the arm factor removes the mean but not heteroskedastic structure.
families.name: post_loss_requeue_latency
families.opportunity_definition: Log seconds between the end of a match and the start of the next in-session match.
families.player_question: When you lose, do you jump straight back into queue or take a breath?
families.story_example: "You re-queue 22% faster after a loss than after a win — you are a chaser."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; transition inside one session.
families.why_care: Re-queue speed is a decision the player fully controls, and it is the behavioural core of what people call tilt-queuing.
families.why_players_differ: Re-queue latency is a personal habit; some people rage-queue and some walk away, and the corpus can see it.

families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted probability that another match follows within the session, after a loss versus after a win.
families.expected_information_reach: Medium: binary, but with several hundred opportunities per player.
families.known_failure_mode: Session boundary is a 3 h modelling choice; the estimand is partly a definition artefact and must be shown stable across gap thresholds before shipping.
families.name: post_loss_session_continuation
families.opportunity_definition: Every product-context match except the last observed one, labelled by whether another match followed within 3 h.
families.player_question: Does a loss make you keep playing, or make you stop for the day?
families.story_example: "A loss makes you 11 points more likely to queue again — you almost never end a night on a defeat."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; the final observed match is right-censored and dropped.
families.unit_of_observation: Match with a known continuation status (not the last observed match).
families.why_care: Whether you end the night on a loss or chase it back is the most consequential session decision a player makes.
families.why_players_differ: Quit discipline is close to a personality trait and is not implied by skill.

confounders: single-draft and random-draft modes remove the choice
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted probability the next hero differs, after a loss versus after a win.
families.known_failure_mode: Single-draft and random-draft matches make the hero non-chosen; they are a small share but must be excluded or modelled before shipping.
families.name: post_loss_hero_switch
families.opportunity_definition: Indicator that the next in-session match uses a different hero.
families.patch_sensitivity: Medium — hero pools shift with patches.
families.player_question: After a loss, do you change hero or run it back?
families.story_example: "After a loss you switch hero 9 points more often than after a win."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; transition inside one session.
families.why_care: Changing or keeping the hero after a loss is a visible, deliberate choice players recognise in themselves.
families.why_players_differ: Some players retreat to a comfort hero after a loss and some abandon the hero that lost; both are stable dispositions.

confounders: players who only ever play one mode have no opportunity
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted probability the next match changes mode stratum, after a loss versus after a win.
families.expected_information_reach: Low to medium; the switch rate is low for most players.
families.expected_structural_reach: Medium — a single-mode player contributes no variation, and single-mode players are common.
families.known_failure_mode: Degenerate for single-mode players: reach is structurally bounded by mode mix, which is itself a strong player trait, so the family risks measuring mode mix rather than response.
families.name: post_loss_mode_switch
families.opportunity_definition: Indicator that the next in-session match's mode stratum differs.
families.player_question: When a game goes badly, do you drop down to Turbo?
families.story_example: "Two losses in and you are in Turbo — you switch modes after a loss twice as often as after a win."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; transition inside one session.
families.why_care: Switching modes after a loss is a recognisable coping move and is invisible on any normal stats page.
families.why_players_differ: Mode mix is a taste; whether a setback moves it is a distinct disposition.

confounders: hero and position change between matches
deaths are partly a team outcome
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted deaths per ten minutes in the next match, after a loss versus after a win.
families.known_failure_mode: Deaths per minute is close to a role signal; without position control (parsed-only) the contrast may be picking up post-loss position change rather than risk.
families.name: post_loss_risk_shift
families.opportunity_definition: Deaths per ten minutes of the following in-session match.
families.parsed_dependency: None; own death *timings* are absent from the corpus but the death count is a history field.
families.player_question: After you lose, does your next game get more reckless?
families.role_position_breadth: All roles, but death rate is strongly position-linked, so position drift between matches is a real confounder.
families.story_example: "Your death rate climbs 12% in the game after a loss."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; transition inside one session.
families.why_care: "I threw the next one" is the folk theory; death exposure is the observable part of it.
families.why_players_differ: Tilt expression differs: some players get passive after a loss, some get reckless.

confounders: sessions end because of losses, so late-half membership is outcome-dependent
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted win indicator between the late half and the early half of a session.
families.expected_information_reach: Low: binary outcome, few long sessions per player.
families.known_failure_mode: Length-biased sampling: a session continues *because* it is going well, so the early/late contrast is endogenous to the outcome being measured.
families.name: session_drift_outcome
families.opportunity_definition: Each match labelled early or late within its own session.
families.player_question: Do you get better or worse as a session goes on?
families.story_example: "Your win rate in the back half of a session is 5 points below the front half."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; sessions of length four or more; middle match dropped when the length is odd.
families.unit_of_observation: Match inside a session of at least four matches.
families.why_care: Everyone believes something about their own stamina; almost nobody has evidence.
families.why_players_differ: Stamina, tilt accumulation, and warm-up curves plausibly differ.

confounders: hero and position drift within a session
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted kill-plus-assist involvement per ten minutes, late half versus early half.
families.expected_information_reach: Medium-high — continuous, many matches per player.
families.known_failure_mode: Kill-plus-assist per minute is partly a team-tempo quantity; a player who switches to support late in a session will look like a fader.
families.name: session_drift_activity
families.opportunity_definition: Involvement per ten minutes for each match, labelled early or late.
families.patch_sensitivity: Medium — kill volume per game is patch-sensitive, but the estimand is a within-session contrast.
families.player_question: Do you stay as involved in fights late in a session as you were at the start?
families.role_position_breadth: All roles; involvement level differs strongly by role so the role mix within a session matters.
families.story_example: "Your fight involvement drops 8% in the back half of long sessions."
families.structural_eligibility: As above.
families.unit_of_observation: Match inside a session of at least four matches.
families.why_care: An involvement fade is something a player can actually act on: it says stop after four, not after seven.
families.why_players_differ: Fatigue expression is individual and shows up in a continuous quantity long before it shows up in win rate.

families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted deaths per ten minutes, late half versus early half.
families.known_failure_mode: Highly redundant with session_drift_activity; the portfolio can carry at most one session-drift response variable.
families.name: session_drift_risk
families.opportunity_definition: Deaths per ten minutes for each match, labelled early or late.
families.player_question: Do you die more as a session wears on?
families.story_example: "You die 15% more often in the back half of a session."
families.structural_eligibility: As above.
families.unit_of_observation: Match inside a session of at least four matches.
families.why_care: It is the most legible fatigue signal in the game.
families.why_players_differ: Concentration decay differs between people.

confounders: first match of a session is disproportionately a solo queue
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted involvement per ten minutes between the first match of a session and the rest.
families.expected_information_reach: Medium-high — the control arm is large.
families.known_failure_mode: Overlaps session_drift_activity mechanically; the two must be shown to separate before both are carried.
families.name: warmup_first_match
families.opportunity_definition: Each match labelled first-of-session or later.
families.player_question: Do you need a warm-up game before you play like yourself?
families.story_example: "Your first game of the night runs 9% below the rest — you are a slow starter."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; sessions of length three or more.
families.unit_of_observation: Match inside a session of at least three matches.
families.why_care: It is directly actionable and distinct from a gradual fade: it is a level shift at the first game only.
families.why_players_differ: Some people arrive ready and some need a game; this is a claim about the shape, not the level.

confounders: patch changes across a long break
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted involvement per ten minutes, returning match versus steady-state match.
families.expected_information_reach: Low: the treated arm is small for exactly the most active players.
families.expected_structural_reach: Medium — a heavy daily player has few three-day breaks.
families.known_failure_mode: Treated-arm scarcity is anti-correlated with the population we can serve; and the patch confound is structural, not incidental.
families.name: layoff_return
families.opportunity_definition: Involvement per ten minutes labelled return or steady.
families.patch_sensitivity: High — long breaks straddle patches by construction.
families.player_question: How do you play the first game back after a few days away?
families.story_example: "Your first game back after a break is 11% quieter than usual."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; gaps between 3 h and 3 days are dropped so the arms are clean.
families.unit_of_observation: Match preceded either by an in-session gap or by a gap of at least three days.
families.why_care: Players constantly wonder whether time off helps or hurts; here it is measurable.
families.why_players_differ: Rust versus refreshment is genuinely individual.

confounders: queue time by region and time of day
no region field exists in the corpus
families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted log gap between matches.
families.known_failure_mode: A level family with no contrast is a population-position statement dressed as a Finding; it also partly measures the player's region and hardware, not the player.
families.name: requeue_tempo
families.opportunity_definition: Log seconds between one match ending and the next starting.
families.player_question: How fast do you start the next game once one ends?
families.story_example: "You are back in queue within 90 seconds — faster than almost anyone we look at."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; in-session transitions.
families.why_care: It is a clean, self-recognisable rhythm, and it frames the post-loss family.
families.why_players_differ: Queue rhythm is a habit, though part of it is server-side.

confounders: window truncation for nine flagged accounts
families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted log session length in matches.
families.known_failure_mode: This is a descriptive fact about someone's calendar, not a behavioural response; it belongs in reference context, not in a Finding.
families.name: session_length
families.opportunity_definition: Log number of matches in the session.
families.player_question: How long do your sessions run once you sit down?
families.story_example: "Your median session is five games long."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; every session including single-match sessions.
families.why_care: It frames every other session claim.
families.why_players_differ: It varies enormously — but it is lifestyle, not gameplay identity.

confounders: no timezone or region field exists, so the block is defined relative to the player's own modal hour
off-peak play may be a different party
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted involvement per ten minutes between the player's own off-peak four-hour block and the rest.
families.expected_information_reach: Low: the off-peak arm is by construction the player's thinnest block.
families.known_failure_mode: Defining off-peak as the block opposite the peak is arbitrary; the treated arm is smallest exactly where it needs to be largest.
families.name: offpeak_shift
families.opportunity_definition: Every match labelled by whether its UTC hour falls in the player's own off-peak block.
families.player_question: Do you play differently in your own off-hours?
families.story_example: "Your late-block games run 14% quieter than your prime-time games."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; players with at least 24 matches so the peak block is identifiable.
families.why_care: "Never queue at 2 a.m." is advice a player can use — if it is true for them.
families.why_players_differ: Chronotype and discipline differ.

confounders: no timezone field, so the weekend boundary is UTC and wrong for many players
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted involvement per ten minutes, weekend versus weekday.
families.known_failure_mode: UTC weekend boundaries are wrong without a timezone; and the effect is expected to be near-zero for nearly everyone, which is not identity.
families.name: weekend_shift
families.opportunity_definition: Every match labelled weekend or weekday in UTC.
families.player_question: Are your weekend games a different kind of game?
families.story_example: "Your weekend games look identical to your weekday games."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows.
families.why_care: Low: it is a calendar fact more than a behavioural one.
families.why_players_differ: Weakly; most players' weekend games are the same games.

confounders: total match volume mechanically lowers novelty rate
random and single draft force novelty
new heroes released in a patch
families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted rate of playing a hero unseen in the previous 30 days.
families.known_failure_mode: Mechanically anti-correlated with match volume, so it partly measures how much someone plays; the rate must be volume-adjusted before shipping.
families.name: hero_novelty
families.opportunity_definition: Indicator that the hero was not played in the previous 30 days.
families.patch_sensitivity: Medium — patch releases create novelty for everyone at once.
families.player_question: Do you keep reaching for heroes you have not touched in a month?
families.story_example: "One game in nine is a hero you have not touched in a month."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; first 30 matches used only to build history.
families.why_care: Explorer versus loyalist is a real identity axis and it is not a skill claim.
families.why_players_differ: Hero-pool breadth is one of the most individual things about a Dota player.

confounders: hero strength differs between pool and non-pool heroes
the pool is chosen, so selection is endogenous
families.directionality: Two-sided; a small gap is the interesting direction.
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted win indicator between comfort-pool heroes and heroes outside it, where the pool is built from strictly prior matches.
families.known_failure_mode: Hero fixed effects are in the context projection, which absorbs much of the very contrast being estimated; and a binary outcome cannot carry a two-point effect at these sample sizes.
families.name: transfer_outcome
families.opportunity_definition: Each match labelled comfort or stretch by the causal pool.
families.player_question: How much does your result depend on being on a comfort hero?
families.story_example: "Off your top five you win only two points less often — your game travels."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; comfort pool is the five most-played heroes to date.
families.why_care: "What survives when the hero changes" is the V6 Transfer question and players ask it constantly.
families.why_players_differ: Some players are their heroes and some are not.

confounders: stretch heroes are played in different modes
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted involvement per ten minutes, stretch heroes versus comfort-pool heroes.
families.known_failure_mode: Hero is a context factor, so the projection removes hero-intrinsic involvement; whatever is left may be tiny, and if hero is dropped from the controls the estimand becomes a hero-strength effect.
families.name: transfer_activity
families.opportunity_definition: Involvement per ten minutes labelled comfort or stretch.
families.player_question: Does your fight involvement hold up on a hero you barely play?
families.story_example: "On unfamiliar heroes your involvement barely moves — you bring the same game."
families.structural_eligibility: As above.
families.why_care: It says whether your playstyle is portable or hero-shaped — a genuinely identity-like claim.
families.why_players_differ: Playstyle portability is a real and personal thing.

confounders: death rate is strongly hero- and position-linked
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted deaths per ten minutes, stretch versus comfort.
families.known_failure_mode: Same hero-absorption problem as the other Transfer variants; also highly redundant with them.
families.name: transfer_risk
families.opportunity_definition: Deaths per ten minutes labelled comfort or stretch.
families.player_question: Do you die more when you step off your comfort heroes?
families.story_example: "Off your comfort heroes you die 18% more — experimenting costs you."
families.structural_eligibility: As above.
families.why_care: It quantifies the real cost of experimenting.
families.why_players_differ: Risk calibration on unfamiliar heroes differs.

confounders: position mix is not controlled without parsed data
families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted deaths per ten minutes.
families.known_failure_mode: Without position control this is largely a position-mix statistic, and a level family invites a good/bad reading; it is closer to a percentile than a Finding.
families.name: risk_appetite
families.opportunity_definition: Deaths per ten minutes.
families.parsed_dependency: None; adding position control makes it parsed-dependent.
families.player_question: Relative to your own context, do you play on the front foot or hold back?
families.role_position_breadth: All roles but strongly position-driven, and position mix is itself behaviour.
families.story_example: "You die a third more often than your heroes and modes would predict — you play forward."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows.
families.why_care: A two-sided tempo axis players recognise instantly.
families.why_players_differ: Risk tolerance is a core play-style axis.

families.directionality: Two-sided in principle, one-sided in perception.
families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted kill-plus-assist involvement per ten minutes.
families.known_failure_mode: This is KDA dressed as identity and reads as a skill percentile; carried only as a redundancy reference for the other involvement families.
families.name: involvement_level
families.opportunity_definition: Involvement per ten minutes.
families.player_question: Are you in more fights than your heroes and modes predict?
families.story_example: "Your involvement runs above what your heroes predict."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows.
families.why_care: Moderate — but it sits very close to raw performance.
families.why_players_differ: Because they play different positions and at different skill levels — which is the problem.

confounders: none material; side assignment is matchmaker-controlled
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted win indicator, Radiant versus Dire.
families.expected_information_reach: High opportunity count, near-zero true signal.
families.known_failure_mode: If this family shows apparent heterogeneity, the screen's variance decomposition is optimistic and every other number in the table needs discounting.
families.name: side_sensitivity
families.opportunity_definition: Every match labelled by side.
families.player_question: Do you play better on one side of the map?
families.story_example: Not a shippable Finding.
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows; side is excluded from the context controls so it can be the arm.
families.why_care: They should not, and that is the point: this family exists to calibrate the screen.
families.why_players_differ: They should not, beyond sampling noise.

families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted log match duration.
families.known_failure_mode: A ten-player outcome attributed to one player; also the most patch-driven quantity available.
families.name: duration_tempo
families.opportunity_definition: Log duration, controlling for result so that the estimand is not a win-rate restatement.
families.patch_sensitivity: High — game length is one of the most patch-sensitive quantities in Dota.
families.player_question: Do your games end faster than comparable games?
families.story_example: "Your games run four minutes shorter than comparable games."
families.structural_eligibility: Product-context rows.
families.why_care: Weak — game length is a ten-player outcome.
families.why_players_differ: Mostly they do not; one player has limited leverage on game length.

families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted normalised-progress centroid of own kill and assist event times.
families.expected_information_reach: High — a bounded continuous quantity with many events per match.
families.expected_structural_reach: Product-wide high; research reach limited to the 116 DISCOVERY parsed accounts.
families.known_failure_mode: Assist timings enter the shape; if the assist stream is systematically incomplete for some matches the centroid is biased, and the corpus tells us the assist *count* is unreliable.
families.name: fight_timing_centroid
families.opportunity_definition: Mean of own event times divided by match duration.
families.parsed_dependency: Full: parsed event timings and role context.
families.player_question: Is your impact concentrated early or late in a game?
families.role_position_breadth: All five positions; the level differs sharply by position so position control is essential.
families.story_example: "Your fights cluster in the first third of the game — you are an early-tempo player."
families.structural_eligibility: Parsed rows joined to a product-context history row; parsed detail present.
families.unit_of_observation: Parsed product-context match with at least three own fight events.
families.why_care: Early-game player versus late-game player is a genuine identity, and Turbo/standard pooling only works because the scale is normalised game progress.
families.why_players_differ: Timing preference is a strong, stable style axis.

families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted normalised progress of the first own kill or assist event.
families.expected_information_reach: Medium — a first-order statistic is noisier than a centroid.
families.known_failure_mode: Strongly redundant with the centroid, and a minimum statistic is dominated by a single lucky event.
families.name: first_fight_timing
families.opportunity_definition: Earliest own event time divided by duration.
families.player_question: How early do you get involved?
families.story_example: "Your first fight lands at 11% of game time — earlier than almost anyone."
families.structural_eligibility: As above.
families.unit_of_observation: Parsed product-context match with at least one own fight event.
families.why_care: A crisp, single-number habit.
families.why_players_differ: Early aggression is individual.

confounders: games that swing are systematically different games
fights happen more when behind because the enemy is pushing
the ±5,000 threshold means different things in Turbo
families.directionality: Two-sided; both fighting on and fading are real styles.
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted own fight events per minute of state, behind versus ahead, where behind and ahead are own-team net-worth lead beyond ±5,000 gold.
families.expected_information_reach: Medium-high — continuous, two rows per match.
families.expected_structural_reach: Bounded by the parsed subset; within it, most matches that swing qualify.
families.known_failure_mode: The fixed ±5,000 gold cut is a wall-clock-like choice on a Turbo/standard-pooled sample; a mode-relative or progress-relative threshold is the correct final form and this discovery version has not yet made that change.
families.name: state_responsive_participation
families.opportunity_definition: Two rows per qualifying match: events per behind-minute and events per ahead-minute.
families.parsed_dependency: Full: net-worth trajectory plus own event timings.
families.patch_sensitivity: Medium; the gold threshold is patch- and mode-sensitive and should be expressed on a mode-relative scale before shipping.
families.player_question: When your team falls behind, do you fight more or go quiet?
families.role_position_breadth: All five positions; supports fight less in both states, so position control matters.
families.story_example: "When your team is 5k down you fight *more*, not less — you are a player who tries to swing it back."
families.structural_eligibility: Parsed rows joined to a product-context history row; both states must occur in the same match, which makes the contrast within-match.
families.unit_of_observation: Parsed product-context match containing at least three clearly-behind and three clearly-ahead minutes.
families.why_care: This is the closest thing the corpus offers to a mental-game Finding that is not a moral judgement: it is a two-sided style claim about how you respond to a losing position.
families.why_players_differ: Response to a losing position is a plausible and player-facing disposition, not a skill level.

confounders: minutes within a match are strongly dependent, so nominal opportunity counts overstate information
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted own fight events per state minute, behind versus ahead.
families.expected_information_reach: Nominally much higher, but minute-level dependence means the effective information is far below the raw count.
families.known_failure_mode: Within-match minute dependence inflates apparent precision; only one of the two sampling variants may enter the portfolio.
families.name: state_responsive_participation_minutes
families.opportunity_definition: One row per state minute rather than one row per match-arm, so the player's arm mean becomes a ratio of sums instead of a mean of small-denominator ratios.
families.player_question: When your team falls behind, do you fight more or go quiet?
families.story_example: Same story as state_responsive_participation.
families.structural_eligibility: Identical to state_responsive_participation.
families.unit_of_observation: One clearly-behind or clearly-ahead minute of a parsed product-context match.
families.why_care: Same behavioural question as state_responsive_participation; recorded separately because it is a materially different sampling model rather than a cosmetic change.
families.why_players_differ: Identical to state_responsive_participation.

confounders: purchase count includes consumables, so it is partly a support/core signal
item identity and tiering are unverified in this corpus
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted item purchases per minute of state, behind versus ahead.
families.expected_information_reach: High — purchases are frequent, median 25 per match.
families.known_failure_mode: Being behind causally reduces gold income, so a population-wide drop is guaranteed; only the *between-player* deviation from that population effect is a Finding, and the estimand must be read that way.
families.name: state_responsive_purchasing
families.opportunity_definition: Two rows per qualifying match: purchases per behind-minute and per ahead-minute.
families.player_question: When you are behind, do you keep farming and buying, or does your economy stall?
families.provider_and_report_cost: Parsed detail required; 3.75 M purchase events in the corpus. Moderate compute.
families.role_position_breadth: All five positions; supports buy far more consumables, so position control is essential.
families.story_example: "Behind by 5k your buying rate barely drops — your economy does not tilt."
families.structural_eligibility: As above.
families.unit_of_observation: Parsed product-context match with at least three behind and three ahead minutes.
families.why_care: It separates players who keep a game going from players whose game collapses with the scoreline — and it never needs to know what the item was.
families.why_players_differ: Economic discipline under pressure is individual, and it is invisible on any scoreboard.

families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted ratio of own kill events to own-team kills.
families.known_failure_mode: After position control there may be little left; before it, the family is a role restatement.
families.name: kill_share
families.opportunity_definition: Own kill-event count divided by own-team kill total. Assist events are excluded on purpose: their count disagrees with the history table in 48% of rows.
families.player_question: What share of your team's kills do you take yourself?
families.role_position_breadth: All five positions but overwhelmingly position-determined.
families.story_example: "You take a third of your team's kills from position four — unusual for the role."
families.structural_eligibility: Parsed rows joined to product context; own-team kill total at least eight.
families.unit_of_observation: Parsed product-context match with at least eight own-team kills.
families.why_care: It separates finishers from enablers without calling either one better.
families.why_players_differ: Largely because they play different positions — which is the risk.

families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted normalised progress at the eighth item purchase.
families.known_failure_mode: The eighth purchase is an arbitrary landmark over an unverified item vocabulary, so it mixes consumables and real items; the atlas rates item semantics MEDIUM and unverified.
families.name: purchase_tempo
families.opportunity_definition: Progress at the eighth purchase event.
families.patch_sensitivity: Medium — item costs move with patches.
families.player_question: How far into a game are you when your build comes together?
families.story_example: "Your eighth item lands at 30% of game time."
families.structural_eligibility: As above.
families.unit_of_observation: Parsed product-context match with at least eight purchases.
families.why_care: Build pace is a real rhythm, and normalised progress makes it comparable across Turbo and standard.
families.why_players_differ: Farming rhythm is individual.

confounders: the lane outcome is a *team-level* verdict on that lane, not the player's own
roamers and junglers have no lane
ties are dropped, which is a third of lanes
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted own fight events per ten minutes of the second half of game progress, lost lane versus won lane.
families.expected_structural_reach: Parsed subset, further reduced by TIE lanes and missing lane assignment.
families.known_failure_mode: The trigger is a team-level lane verdict, so a player can be assigned a lost lane they personally won; this attribution error is not recoverable from this corpus.
families.name: lane_recovery_participation
families.opportunity_definition: Own event count in the second half of game progress, scaled to a ten-minute rate.
families.parsed_dependency: Full, plus lane-outcome semantics rated MEDIUM in the atlas.
families.player_question: When your lane loses, do you still show up in the second half of the game?
families.role_position_breadth: Three lanes only; jungle and roaming are too sparse to carry it.
families.story_example: "Even when your lane loses, your second-half presence holds — you do not fold."
families.structural_eligibility: Parsed rows joined to product context; lane must be SAFE/OFF/MID and the lane outcome must not be TIE.
families.unit_of_observation: Parsed product-context match with a decided lane outcome for the player's own lane.
families.why_care: Recovering from a bad lane is the most common thing a Dota player has to do.
families.why_players_differ: Resilience after a bad start is plausibly individual.

confounders: a lost lane is a lost lane for the whole team
families.directionality: Two-sided; a small gap is the interesting direction.
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted win indicator, lost lane versus won lane.
families.expected_information_reach: Low: binary response on a reduced sample.
families.known_failure_mode: Almost no player-level heterogeneity is plausible: losing your lane is bad for everyone by roughly the same amount.
families.name: lane_recovery_outcome
families.opportunity_definition: Win indicator labelled by own-lane outcome.
families.player_question: How much does a lost lane cost you in the end?
families.story_example: "A lost lane costs you 20 points of win rate — about average."
families.structural_eligibility: As above.
families.unit_of_observation: Parsed product-context match with a decided own-lane outcome.
families.why_care: It is the version of the question players actually ask.
families.why_players_differ: Weakly: the lane outcome largely determines the game for everyone.

confounders: the trajectory is a team quantity shared with four teammates
families.estimand: Per-player difference in context-adjusted win indicator between decided-ahead and decided-behind midpoints.
families.expected_information_reach: Low: binary and heavily saturated — most decided leads convert.
families.known_failure_mode: A team outcome attributed to one player, with a saturated binary response; expected to show near-zero player heterogeneity, which is exactly what learning 9 says to reject.
families.name: lead_retention
families.opportunity_definition: Win indicator labelled by the sign of the midpoint lead.
families.patch_sensitivity: High — comeback mechanics are a patch lever.
families.player_question: When your team is clearly ahead at the midpoint, do your games close out?
families.story_example: "You convert 5k leads at 88% — the usual rate."
families.structural_eligibility: Parsed rows joined to product context; trajectory of at least eight minutes.
families.unit_of_observation: Parsed product-context match whose midpoint net-worth lead exceeds ±5,000 gold.
families.why_care: Throwing leads is the most emotionally loaded pattern in Dota.
families.why_players_differ: Barely: one of five players has limited leverage on whether a 5k lead converts.

confounders: fights are denser in losing positions for everyone
the sign of the lead is a coarse state
families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted difference between the share of own events landing in behind-minutes and the share of the game spent behind.
families.known_failure_mode: Strongly redundant with state_responsive_participation, which uses a sharper state definition; the portfolio can carry one, not both.
families.name: comeback_participation
families.opportunity_definition: Event share minus exposure share, so the population baseline is zero by construction.
families.player_question: Are you more or less present than usual while your team is behind?
families.story_example: "A third more of your fight involvement happens while behind than the clock alone would give you."
families.structural_eligibility: Parsed rows joined to product context.
families.unit_of_observation: Parsed product-context match with at least four own events and both behind and ahead minutes.
families.why_care: It is the deficit half of game-state responsiveness, expressed as a share so it is immune to how long the game was behind.
families.why_players_differ: Presence under pressure is individual.

families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted own events per minute in the first quarter of game progress.
families.known_failure_mode: Redundant with the fight-timing centroid, and a rate rather than a shape means it leans towards a performance reading.
families.name: early_fight_rate
families.opportunity_definition: Own events at progress ≤ 0.25, per minute of that span.
families.player_question: How busy are your first ten minutes?
families.story_example: "Your first ten minutes are twice as busy as your position predicts."
families.structural_eligibility: Parsed rows joined to product context.
families.why_care: Early tempo is a recognisable style.
families.why_players_differ: Early aggression is stable and personal.

confounders: parsed availability must hold for *both* matches, which compounds the selection
hero is in the controls and is nearly collinear with position
families.estimand: Per-player mean context-adjusted probability that the position changes between consecutive in-session matches.
families.expected_structural_reach: Parsed subset, further reduced by the consecutive-pair requirement.
families.known_failure_mode: Hero is in the context controls and is close to collinear with position, so the projection may absorb most of the signal; and requiring two consecutive parsed matches compounds parsed selection.
families.name: position_flexibility
families.opportunity_definition: Indicator that the position differs from the previous in-session match.
families.parsed_dependency: Full and doubled: two parsed matches in a row.
families.player_question: Do you play the same position game after game, or rotate?
families.story_example: "Four games in five you change position — you are the fill player."
families.structural_eligibility: Two consecutive product-context matches, both parsed, inside one session.
families.why_care: The median account has played all five positions, so position mix is behaviour rather than an attribute — and flexibility is a real identity.
families.why_players_differ: Some players are one-position players and some fill; this is a strong and legible axis.

notes: observed between-player spread does not exceed within-player noise: no detectable player heterogeneity at this support
